title: Korean Table Etiquette: Offering, Receiving or Declining a Drink
excerpt: Understand two-handed gestures at the Korean table and use a polite phrase to choose another drink or decline.
content: At a Korean meal, you may see people offer to pour for one another or use two hands when sharing a drink with an older person. These are gestures of courtesy. Everyone can decide what to drink. If you prefer not to have alcohol, you can say so and ask for another drink. Offering and receiving In a more formal setting, use both hands to hold the bottle when offering a pour, or hold your glass with both hands when someone offers to pour for you. [Korea.net's guide to table manners](https://www.korea.net/NewsFocus/Society/view?articleId=175173&pageIndex=1) describes these gestures in relation to older people. You can simply ask before pouring: “Would you like some?” Practices vary between people and occasions. Watch your companions and follow their preferences rather than assuming that someone's age or position means they want a refill. There is no need to keep another person's glass full.

It is not legal advice; the current law and the provider's instructions control. Your right to request your own records Article 21 of Korea's Medical Service Act says a patient may ask a healthcare professional or medical institution to inspect or receive copies of all or part of the records concerning that patient. The institution should not refuse without justifiable grounds. excerpt: Plan post-treatment travel around your own recovery, follow-up needs, medical documents, and the treating clinician's advice.
content: If you receive medical treatment in South Korea and plan to travel afterward, discuss your itinerary with the clinician responsible for your care. Recovery and fitness to fly depend on the individual, the treatment, and any complications. There is no universal number of days that is safe for every procedure.
